If the English, French, Dutch, even the Ottomans had been players in New World colonization at that very early stage, it may have been possible for local peoples to identify, “Okay, these are different cultures. We can play them off against each other to our advantage.” That may have been the game, but at that time, it wasn’t possible.
Dwarkesh Patel

I know you’ve spent a little bit of time thinking about what happened in all these other episodes of colonialism as well. In India, for example, we do have many different European powers. Why was it not possible for the Mughals to play them off each other indefinitely to keep control over India?
Si Sheppard

The Mughals peaked under Aurangzeb at the beginning of the 18th century. Subsequently, his successors didn’t have whatever you call it — the authority, the charisma, the rizz, however you want to define it — to maintain that hegemony which he’d established by almost taking over all of India.

The Mughals always at root had the same problem that the Manchu did when they conquered the Ming in the 17th century and built Qing dynasty China to the greatest physical extent it ever had. They were always outsiders. They were not indigenous to the population. In the background, there was always that vague resentment that “we’re being ruled here by foreigners.” That was okay while they were going from success to success. But when the momentum halts and it begins to roll backwards, that’s when the local power brokers begin to feel to themselves, “Maybe we have more to gain from breaking away from the empire than we do from remaining within it.” Both Mughal India and Manchu China had that kind of fatal defect, as it were, coded into the ultimate basis for their authority.

So even without the Europeans, I think the Mughal Empire would have peaked and it would have disintegrated. What would have happened next would be more like a patchwork quilt of different authorities, some larger, some smaller. The Maratha Confederacy I think would have been a major player, but not one that could incorporate the entire subcontinent within its authority.

Of course, we look at Chinese history. It’s the constant cycle of the rise of a dynasty, its peak, its decline into anarchy, and then the rise of a new imperial hegemon in the region. That cycle would play out, I think, regardless of whether the Europeans intervened.

Specifically in terms of why the British took over at the end, in the bluntest terms, the Royal Navy rules the waves. In terms of projecting power, the Brits were able to force the French out of Canada and out of India because they controlled the sea lanes. Although the French had, in terms of population and military, a larger force, if you can’t project that force, it’s really of no value to you.
Dwarkesh Patel

This is very interesting, because it makes sense why the British could have been one of the major powers in India, where there’s the Marathas, there’s the remainders of the Mughal Empire, there’s many other factions, and then there’s this British outpost. They’ve gotten rid of the French, the British have got Bengal. Why is it that they were able to consolidate where nobody else is able to consolidate?

One hypothesis here is that we often talk about advantages in technology, but we don’t talk about advantages in governance or in terms of organization. The East India Company was a company. It had a board that could fire and hire CEOs and lieutenants and whatever. It wasn’t called a CEO, obviously. It wasn’t necessarily the most competent people who were in charge of the East India Trading Company, though they were pretty competent people, Robert Clive and his underlings.

You would have instances… For example, I think the nawabs of Bengal right before the British are able to gain control of Bengal, which is the initial tax base that they set up in order to further their conquest. Alivardi Khan is considered to be a pretty good ruler who was able to hold the British at bay. Then he dies, and his grandson is this kind of crazy, psychopathic guy who doesn’t listen to advice and so forth. Because there’s this monarchical tradition across all these principalities in India, there’s just going to be, sooner or later, a bad king, and that king will not be able to stop the British incursion.

There are also all these forces around these principalities where it’s, “Who are we going to lend money to? Who are we going to lend our troops to?” They realize there’s a bad king right now. The British seem pretty competent. “I’m going to make an alliance with the British instead.”

Similarly with the case of the Aztecs and the Incas, and maybe even more so, the overwhelming majority of the troops, the forces that the British are using are Indians, sepoys. This is an underrated thing, being able to delegate to competent people and then being able to replace them one after another if they get killed or if they resign or something. There’s not going to be some crazy succession crisis that creates this anarchy that then somebody else can swoop in and take control.
Si Sheppard

Absolutely. Just to give one example, the British were winning the Hundred Years’ War because the King of France, Charles VI, was insane. He was convinced he was made out of glass, for example. Then the English lost the Hundred Years’ War because their king, Henry VI, was insane, and he would just shut down for months at a time. Mentally, he just couldn’t function.

In non-democratic environments, yes, the corporations, for the reasons you outlined — profit-driven and therefore not loyal to bloodlines or any other kind of extraneous circumstances, but just looking for the most competent leadership and a capacity to change and replace people — are much more flexible than those kind of hierarchical states. Even in many ways, you could argue, in democratic societies the corporations can still outmaneuver them because they’re untied to particular loyalties, and it’s just their brand awareness that they’re trying to push.

The British and Dutch were late to the game of imperialism. You wouldn’t give them much of a chance given the differentials, but they unleashed the power of the free market. As you say, the East India Company, the English and Dutch equivalents, the British Hudson’s Bay Company, which is really what made Canada as we understand it today… Those corporations, driven by those motives, acting with almost plenipotentiary powers at vast distances, had the flexibility on the ground to take advantage of local circumstances, to insert themselves into diplomatic arrangements which had persisted for centuries with all the accumulated grievances. Here were the fresh newcomers: “We obviously have skills at what we do.”

As you say, taking control of the tax revenue of Bengal effectively took control of the entire political orbit. What can you do without taxation? Reorient that towards the shareholders, force the local people to stop producing these crops, even if it means millions starve to death, in order to produce opium to take advantage of that. It was devastating in its impact in political structures that had no real environment where that was part of their established traditions.

Even the conquistadors, even the Vikings, if we go back far enough, these were business operations. The Vikings would be men who would assemble with what weapons they had, enough capital upfront to pay for boats to go raiding, to make this profitable by looting churches and monasteries.

That’s what the conquistadors were. They were freebooters operating within a capitalist system. These were not desperados of the lowest of the low. Many of them had some education. A lot of them were hidalgos, which is the lowest rung of the petty nobility in Castile, who inherited titles and attitudes, but not much in assets beyond what they could put up as soldiers of fortune. They called themselves compañeros, which is colleagues or companions, not soldados. This whole operation was, if you like, the most raw, unbridled capitalism at its finest, pooling assets to derive enormous profits from very risky ventures.
Dwarkesh Patel

Maybe to close us off, the thing I find really remarkable in these stories… We’ve talked about how lopsided these battles have been, how quickly this conquest proceeded. In the grand scheme of things, the technological advantages that the conquistadors had over these empires are not that shockingly big. As you mentioned, guns at this time are not good enough to actually be that helpful during battle, so it’s basically horses and steel weapons. In fact, I don’t know if we’ve talked about this, but towards the ends of these conquests, or the middles of these conquests, the metal is weighing them down and it’s really hot and stuff. So they’re even reverting to the cotton armor that the natives are using. So it’s not even the armor.

It’s really just that they had better metal swords instead of obsidian blades, and that they had horses. That’s enough to let a couple hundred men take over entire empires. You can draw analogies to what might happen in the future. We don’t even have to go there. I just find it remarkable how little it took for them to be so dominant.
Si Sheppard

They could win battles. They could not have won the war, though, at the end without the support of those indigenous allies. So those are all the numbers. Yes, you’re actually right. They would almost keep the helmets to protect the head, but many of them were ditching the metal armor in favor of the local stuff because that was good enough as protection against local weapons. They would not have done that and carried it back to Europe. That would have made them too vulnerable. But here you adapt to the circumstances. You have more freedom of mobility. It’s less exhausting wearing cotton than it is to wear metal. They would make that adaptation.

They would even sometimes, for very prized allies, again as a way of integrating them into the Spanish coalition, provide local chiefs and warlords with Spanish weapons, just to emphasize, “You’re so special to me.” This was effective in binding them together. They were very, very clever in identifying the local sub-chiefs beneath the Aztec layer of authority who would be receptive to the idea of, “Why are you taking orders from them when you get a better deal from us?”

They knew, for example, the Aztec Empire was called the Triple Alliance because it was set up in 1428 by the first huey tlatoani as a coalition between the three city-states: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tacuba.

In 1516, so three years before Cortés arrived in Mesoamerica, the chief, or king, of Texcoco died, and his two sons fought a civil war for who would succeed him. Moctezuma stepped in and gave the title to one of those brothers. So what does the other brother do when the Spanish show up? He immediately sides with them. His own family was on both sides of this war. This is his path to getting what he feels is his due, being the king of Texcoco. In the broader sense, “If I’m under the Spanish versus under the Aztecs, maybe these newcomers will give me a better deal.” There was that seductive quality at the elite level.

Now, what they didn’t understand — so many of them thinking they were using the Spanish to their advantage — they didn’t appreciate the numbers in which the Spanish and later Europeans would arrive. Their closed worlds didn’t allow them to think that people from such vast distances could come in such huge numbers. In the end, as happened in, for example, Australia and New Zealand, “We’ll become the minority in our own country.” The demographic tide they didn’t appreciate in the long term would work fundamentally against them.
Dwarkesh Patel

The analogy to AI there is so obvious it’s not worth spelling out. But that’s actually an excellent place to close. This is such a bizarre and shocking and interesting part of human history, and I appreciate you coming on and telling us all about it.
Si Sheppard
Real pleasure. Thank you for having me.

articles.title: The day GIF became free to use, forever
articles.titleZh: The day GIF became free to use, forever
articles.summary: The day GIF became free to use, forever

blocks.text: October 1, 2006 was a good day. It was the day that the last of the patents covering the GIF file format finally expired and GIF became free to use. Today GIF is a staple of social media, but it was also a staple of the early web, and, indeed, telecommunications before the Internet became accessible to the average household.
Origins of GIF

Originally, GIF was a file format developed by CompuServe and released in June 1987 to provide a cross-platform graphics format their subscribers could use to share graphics online. The format caught on and proliferated throughout online services and bulletin boards. Almost anyone who was online prior to the World Wide Web becoming popular downloaded at least one GIF file at some point. GIF was free for anyone to use as far as CompuServe was concerned, at least in those early days.

When the World Wide Web came along in the early ’90s and made the Internet more accessible to all, GIF was one of the graphics file formats it supported. It was widely understood, it had widespread software support, gave excellent compression on images that didn’t originate as photos, and it decompressed and rendered faster than JPEG because it originated at a time when 8 MHz was a fast CPU. In fact, the web supported GIF before it supported JPEG.

It was unusual to visit a Web page in 1994 and for it to not have at least one GIF image in it. Early web designers used them to provide graphical elements to break up the wall of text, but we also used them in more subtle ways. One example was using them as a background pattern. By default, the Web was black text on a gray background. Designers would make patterns to make the background a little more visually interesting than one of 216 solid background colors. Technically, any computer on the Web could display at least 256 colors, but there were 216 of them that were always the same regardless of browser and platform. Creating seamlessly repeating textures that used combinations of those 216 colors was an easy way to dress up a Web page in the early days.
The invisible GIF hack

But it wasn’t long before the GIF took on another important element. Early HTML didn’t give a lot of control over the text. You could change the font, you could boldface some or all of it, and you could do the same for italics and underlining, and you could change the size. But you didn’t really have the degree of control over it that graphic designers were used to having in other media.

The trick was to use a single pixel transparent GIF file as a spacer. You could drop that image anywhere on the page and specify a height or width in pixels to force white space there. It was a trick to change the line spacing in your text or to put a variable width space somewhere in your text if you wanted it.

I don’t know who invented this technique. I read about it in a book titled Web Sites that Work by Roger Black and Sean Elder. Here’s a blog post I wrote about that back in 2002. I had at least two different people tell me about Black’s book within 30 days of each other. I had a friend who worked in a bookstore, so he used his employee discount to get me a copy.
It wasn’t long before everyone I knew was using that trick on their web pages. Suddenly, we could do most of things we learned how to do in our graphic design classes on the web. It was great.
A funny story about the invisible GIF

Fast forward a few years. I was using this trick in an early version of this blog, when someone emailed me and accused me of using the blog to spy on him. I asked what he meant. He told me I was using web bugs, and he pointed me to my invisible GIF file. I said I was using that for line spacing and paragraph spacing. He insisted I was using it to track what he was reading.

There were people who used an invisible GIF file to do some tracking. The trick was to host that file on a web server somewhere, embedded in an email message or something else, and then when someone retrieved that file, they would have an entry in your server log.
So it was possible to use the invisible GIF file as a crude tracking mechanism. But that’s not what I was doing. Some things about the Internet never change: Everyone’s an expert.
Painting the whole screen with GIFs

A more extreme design technique was to draw the major design elements of a page in Photoshop, then slice it into smaller GIFs, and reassemble the pieces in HTML. This allowed designers complete control over how the page rendered, including placement of elements and the ability to use any fonts they wanted. The tradeoff was speed. Designers would code pages specially to line the elements up so the page was halfway readable while the GIFs slowly downloaded and populated the screen at dialup speed.
In the example on the right, the old Cyberrebate.com page, everything on the page that wasn’t Times New Roman was a GIF, including the banner, the sidebar, all the logos, and the clickable buttons.
When you pull up an old page on archive.org and see blank squares missing, that’s an artifact of that type of design.
This technique is completely obsolete today but was common in the late 1990s, at least until patents made it dangerous.
Why GIF wasn’t truly free

The problem keeping GIF from being truly free was that it used a compression algorithm, Lempel-Ziv-Welch, or LZW, that was still protected by a patent. When it was just private individuals sharing images with each other, nobody really cared. CompuServe wasn’t aware of the patent at the time it used LZW. But once it started looking like people would start using the Internet for commercial purposes, those patents became a problem. Of course the patent holder, Unisys, was going to try to monetize that.

Commercial graphics software was already paying a royalty on the patent, so it wasn’t necessarily a huge deal for someone using commercial graphics software to create their Web page. But software that didn’t cost anything was another problem. Most software of that type stopped supporting the file format. When Unisys announced owners of non-commercial and private web sites had the “opportunity” to obtain a license for a one-time payment of $5,000 or $7,500, there was understandable backlash.
Alternatives to GIF

Some websites started using the JPEG file format exclusively. But some implementations of JPEG made certain types of images, especially line drawings, look terrible. It would introduce artifacts that made it impossible to draw a straight line, for example.

The PNG file format was a reaction against the GIF patents. The goal was to make a non-lossy file format that used a compression method not covered by any patent. They chose Deflate, the method used by Phil Katz’ ZIP. And while they were at it, they made it possible to support 24-bit images with 16.8 million colors, rather than stopping at 8-bit images with 256 colors. PNG also had transparency.
The only thing it didn’t have was support for animation. I didn’t miss that, but I was probably in the minority on that.

It wasn’t terribly long before HTML matured to the point where you didn’t need hacks involving invisible GIFs to adjust line spacing and position elements on a page. I just got out of the habit of using the file format at all. When I did need a graphical element, I just used JPEG or PNG and got on with life.
I think a lot of other people did the same, so it’s likely the GIF patents didn’t turn into the revenue source everyone expected.
Choosy browsers choose GIF

Unisys’ patents expired worldwide in 2003 and 2004, but IBM held a relevant patent that didn’t expire until 2006. While few really expected IBM to take the hard line Unisys had, given IBM’s problems with SCO, there wasn’t much reason to take chances. On October 1, 2006, that final IBM patent expired. GIF was free for any and all use.

Not long after that last patent expired, animated GIFs came back with a vengeance. It was a convenient file format for sharing short videos on social media. Animation was the one thing GIF did that PNG didn’t. Animated versions of PNG such as APNG existed, but Internet Explorer didn’t support them. Internet Explorer did support GIF, so GIF became the cross-browser animated file format standard by default. When Edge switched to Chromium, it supported all of the file formats Chrome and Firefox did, but GIF had momentum by then. With no financial incentive to switch, GIF stuck this time.
Today it may seem hard to believe that the file format virtually vanished from the Internet for about 10 years. We’re still arguing how to pronounce it though.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

blocks.text:
"Wuthering Heights" by Emily Brontë - good writing, but the protagonists are
quite something. There's barely a likable character in the whole story - they
are all either crazy, evil, stupid or a combination of these. It's also
remarkable to consider how small the world of some people in those times was
(pre-Victorian England); whole lives spent within a tiny area, interacting
with a handful of other people. And that's for members of the nobility, not
some bumpkin on a remote farm.

"The Pickled City: The Story of New York pickles" by Paul Van Ravenstein and
Monique Mulder - yes, a book about pickles, with lots of cool photos! That's
what you get while randomly browsing in the local public library while your
kids are picking out their books. All you wanted to know about the history
of pickles, with particular emphasis on NYC in the early 20th century and
the connection to Jewish immigration to that city.

"Rebel Island: the incredible history of Taiwan" by Jonathan Clements - a
detailed history of Taiwan, focusing mostly on the early years (pre-modern
times). The writing is a bit academic and dry, but it's very comprehensive.
I wish the book spent more time on the modern era, though.

"The Old Ways: A Journey on Foot" by Robert Macfarlane - an ode to taking
long walks (from hours to multi-day hikes). The writing is very beautiful,
but much of it feels pointless; the author describes friends and obscure
historical poets in a lot of detail which has little to do with the main
thesis of the book. I'd say the first 1/4 of the good is very good, and the
rest is unnecessary.

"After Rain" by William Trevor - I'm on a quest to find additional authors
that write evocative short stories that stay with you, and Trevor was
recommended as someone to try since my current favorites are Steinbeck
and Lahiri. "After Rain" is a collection of 12 stories, mostly about love
and relationships - between partners but also parents and children; the
settings are usually in 1980s Ireland or England. Very good stories overall,
I'm glad I tried this author and should try something else by him.

"Spoonhandle" by Ruth Moore - a novel about the lives of Maine natives living
through changing times, seeing their picturesque coastal area become a magnet
for "summer people" - rich vacationers from the big cities. There's no single
protagonist in the book and the writing is very warm and human. I enjoyed it.

"The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World's Most Powerful Money" by
Brendan Greeley - a history-oriented exploration of the importance of the
dollar in world economy, from its beginnings as the Joachimsthaler in 16th
century Bohemia and until modern times. This book has some interesting
ideas but I found it to be quite academical and not easy to digest.

"Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst" by Robert M. Sapolsky
- the scope of this (very long) book is huge: explaining how human behavior
works starting from basic biological principles. Our understanding of the
actual biological underpinnings of behavior is so nascent, however, that
the vast majority of the book focuses on the usual things - the psychological
studies (including all the well known ones like prisoner's dilemma, the
Stanford prison experiment, etc) and comparison with other animals. Having
read several other books on this topic in the past, I haven't found much
new in this one.

"Humorous short stories" by Anton Chekhov (read in Russian) - a collection of
short stories with a humorous angle. The stories are typically very short,
just 2-3 pages each, but the character building is superb. I should try
reading something longer by Chekhov.

"Plainsong" by Kent Haruf - describes a year in the life of several loosely
connected people in a remote farm town in eastern Colorado. A wholesome
story, without a specific beginning or end - just the lives of ordinary
folks.

"Behind the Beautiful Forevers: Life, Death, and Hope in a Mumbai Undercity"
by Katherine Boo - investigative journalism of the lives of several connected
families in Annawadi - one of Mumbai's most miserable slums - roughly from
2007 to 2010. The only thing more shocking than the squalor in which these
people live is the degree of corruption, fraud and exploitation surrounding
them. A very poignant read.

"The Dispossessed" by Ursula K. Le Guin - science fiction only in the sense
of 1984; it's always amusing to examine how unambitious the futuristic vision
of some authors is. The book was written in the early 1970s, and it presents
life thousands of years in the future as one that's pretty much identical to
what it was in the early 1970s, except for close-to-speed-of-light travel. But
science is not the point of this book anyway; it's more of a political or
philosophical fiction, examining an anarchist-communist society and comparing
it to a capitalist, "propertarian" one. Overall, this book gave me very
strong vibes of the famous Soviet kids story "Dunno on the moon" (Незнайка
на Луне), which I recall reading as a kid.

"The Lion Women of Tehran" by Marjan Kamali - a multi-generational novel
focusing on the life of young women in Iran from the early 1950s to the early
1980s, in the context of the various authoritarian governments of those
eras (from Mohammad Reza Pahlavi's rule to after the Islamic revolution of
1979). Nice book showing that a good story can be told without too many
unnecessary twists and classical attention-grabbing dramas.

"The Old Way: A story of the first people" by Elizabeth Marshall Thomas
"Interpreter of Maladies" by Jhumpa Lahiri
"Norwegian Wood" by Haruki Murakami

translations:
"Wuthering Heights" by Emily Brontë - good writing, but the protagonists are
quite something. There's barely a likable character in the whole story - they
are all either crazy, evil, stupid or a combination of these. It's also
remarkable to consider how small the world of some people in those times was
(pre-Victorian England); whole lives spent within a tiny area, interacting
with a handful of other people. And that's for members of the nobility, not
some bumpkin on a remote farm.

"The Pickled City: The Story of New York pickles" by Paul Van Ravenstein and
Monique Mulder - yes, a book about pickles, with lots of cool photos! That's
what you get while randomly browsing in the local public library while your
kids are picking out their books. All you wanted to know about the history
of pickles, with particular emphasis on NYC in the early 20th century and
the connection to Jewish immigration to that city.

"Rebel Island: the incredible history of Taiwan" by Jonathan Clements - a
detailed history of Taiwan, focusing mostly on the early years (pre-modern
times). The writing is a bit academic and dry, but it's very comprehensive.
I wish the book spent more time on the modern era, though.

"The Old Ways: A Journey on Foot" by Robert Macfarlane - an ode to taking
long walks (from hours to multi-day hikes). The writing is very beautiful,
but much of it feels pointless; the author describes friends and obscure
historical poets in a lot of detail which has little to do with the main
thesis of the book. I'd say the first 1/4 of the good is very good, and the
rest is unnecessary.

"After Rain" by William Trevor - I'm on a quest to find additional authors
that write evocative short stories that stay with you, and Trevor was
recommended as someone to try since my current favorites are Steinbeck
and Lahiri. "After Rain" is a collection of 12 stories, mostly about love
and relationships - between partners but also parents and children; the
settings are usually in 1980s Ireland or England. Very good stories overall,
I'm glad I tried this author and should try something else by him.

"Spoonhandle" by Ruth Moore - a novel about the lives of Maine natives living
through changing times, seeing their picturesque coastal area become a magnet
for "summer people" - rich vacationers from the big cities. There's no single
protagonist in the book and the writing is very warm and human. I enjoyed it.

"The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World's Most Powerful Money" by
Brendan Greeley - a history-oriented exploration of the importance of the
dollar in world economy, from its beginnings as the Joachimsthaler in 16th
century Bohemia and until modern times. This book has some interesting
ideas but I found it to be quite academical and not easy to digest.

"Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst" by Robert M. Sapolsky
- the scope of this (very long) book is huge: explaining how human behavior
works starting from basic biological principles. Our understanding of the
actual biological underpinnings of behavior is so nascent, however, that
the vast majority of the book focuses on the usual things - the psychological
studies (including all the well known ones like prisoner's dilemma, the
Stanford prison experiment, etc) and comparison with other animals. Having
read several other books on this topic in the past, I haven't found much
new in this one.

"Humorous short stories" by Anton Chekhov (read in Russian) - a collection of
short stories with a humorous angle. The stories are typically very short,
just 2-3 pages each, but the character building is superb. I should try
reading something longer by Chekhov.

"Plainsong" by Kent Haruf - describes a year in the life of several loosely
connected people in a remote farm town in eastern Colorado. A wholesome
story, without a specific beginning or end - just the lives of ordinary
folks.

"Behind the Beautiful Forevers: Life, Death, and Hope in a Mumbai Undercity"
by Katherine Boo - investigative journalism of the lives of several connected
families in Annawadi - one of Mumbai's most miserable slums - roughly from
2007 to 2010. The only thing more shocking than the squalor in which these
people live is the degree of corruption, fraud and exploitation surrounding
them. A very poignant read.

"The Dispossessed" by Ursula K. Le Guin - science fiction only in the sense
of 1984; it's always amusing to examine how unambitious the futuristic vision
of some authors is. The book was written in the early 1970s, and it presents
life thousands of years in the future as one that's pretty much identical to
what it was in the early 1970s, except for close-to-speed-of-light travel. But
science is not the point of this book anyway; it's more of a political or
philosophical fiction, examining an anarchist-communist society and comparing
it to a capitalist, "propertarian" one. Overall, this book gave me very
strong vibes of the famous Soviet kids story "Dunno on the moon" (Незнайка
на Луне), which I recall reading as a kid.

"The Lion Women of Tehran" by Marjan Kamali - a multi-generational novel
focusing on the life of young women in Iran from the early 1950s to the early
1980s, in the context of the various authoritarian governments of those
eras (from Mohammad Reza Pahlavi's rule to after the Islamic revolution of
1979). Nice book showing that a good story can be told without too many
unnecessary twists and classical attention-grabbing dramas.

"The Old Way: A story of the first people" by Elizabeth Marshall Thomas
"Interpreter of Maladies" by Jhumpa Lahiri
"Norwegian Wood" by Haruki Murakami
"Cannery Row" by John Steinbeck
